'''Joseph Alvin Neisendorfer''' (born April 22, 1945 in [[Chicago]]) is an American mathematician known for his work in [[homotopy theory]], an area of [[algebraic topology]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.math.rochester.edu/people/faculty/jnei/ |title=Neisendorfer Homepage |website=[[University of Rochester]] |access-date=2018-05-17}}</ref> He is a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list |title=List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society |website=American Mathematical Society |access-date=2018-05-17}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Neisendorfer earned his bachelor's degree in 1967 from the [[University of Chicago]]. He earned his master's degree in 1968 and his doctorate in 1972 from [[Princeton University]], working under the direction of [[John Coleman Moore]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=8597}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2016/04/08/john-c-moore-dedicated-and-influential-princeton-mathematician-dies |title=John C. Moore, dedicated and influential Princeton mathematician, dies |last=Kelly |first=Morgan |date=2016-04-08 |website=Princeton University |access-date=2018-05-17}}</ref>

In 1972, he began working as an assistant professor at the [[University of Notre Dame]], then in 1976 at [[Syracuse University]], and then in 1978 at [[Fordham University]]. From September of 1979 to July of 1983, he worked at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]<ref>{{cite web
 | title = Joseph Neisendorfer
 | url = https://www.ias.edu/scholars/joseph-neisendorfer
 | website = Institute for Advanced Study
 | access-date = 22 August 2026
}}</ref> after which he became an associate professor at [[Ohio State University]]. He is now an emeritus professor at the [[University of Rochester]]<ref>{{cite web
 | title = Joseph Neisendorfer
 | url = https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/people/faculty/neisendorfer-joseph/index.html
 | website = Department of Mathematics, University of Rochester
 | access-date = 22 August 2026
}}</ref> where he worked for 26 years from 1985 until his retirement in 2011, serving as department chair from 1994 to 1996. 

During his tenure as the department chair, the [[University of Rochester]] experienced severe financial challenges which led to significant restructuring entitled the Rochester Renaissance Plan.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rochester.edu/news/show.php?id=1838 |title=Rochester Renaissance Plan for The College |website=University of Rochester |date=1995-11-16 |access-date=2018-05-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
 | title = Rochester Renaissance Plan for The College
 | url = https://www.rochester.edu/news/printable.php?id=1838
 | website = University of Rochester
 | date = 16 November 1995
 | access-date = 22 August 2026
}}</ref> In November 1995, the mathematics department was told by the University of Rochester administration that the doctoral program was slated for removal and that the departmental faculty slated for significant downsizing, and admissions to the University of Rochester doctoral program in Mathematics were suspended.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/02/04/nyregion/fears-that-loss-of-a-math-phd-program-figures-in-a-bigger-equation.html |title=Fears That Loss of a Math Ph.D. Program Figures in a Bigger Equation |last=Arenson |first=Karen W. |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=1996-02-04 |access-date=2018-05-17 }}</ref> This decision led to the involvement of the [[American Mathematical Society]], which passed a resolution urging Rochester to reconsider and formed a task force (chaired by [[Arthur Jaffe]]) to address the issue.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/notices/199603/rochester.pdf |title=Downsizing at Rochester: Mathematics Ph.D. Program Cut |journal=[[Notices of the AMS]] |volume=43 |number=3 |pages=300&ndash;306 |last=Jackson |first=Allyn |year=1996}}</ref> After a fact-finding committee organized by Neisendorfer sent its report to the university administration, the doctoral program in mathematics was restored.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rochester.edu/news/show.php?id=1843 |title=Rochester Enhancing Math Programs |website=University of Rochester |date=1996-03-28 |access-date=2018-05-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/publicoutreach/rochester |title=Flash Update from the Rochester Task Force of the AMS |date=1996-03-28 |last=Jaffe |first=Arthur |website=American Mathematical Society |access-date=2018-05-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Neisendorfer |first=Joseph |url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/about/support-usq-maths/letter-from-joseph-niesendorfer/ |title=Letter from Joseph Neisendorfer |website=[[Terence Tao|What's New]] |date=2008-04-10 |access-date=2018-05-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
 | title = Details on the Rochester Renaissance Plan
 | url = https://www.rochester.edu/news/printable.php?id=1839
 | website = University of Rochester
 | date = 16 November 1995
 | access-date = 22 August 2026
}}</ref>

== Mathematics ==

Neisendorfer is best known for a series of influential papers on unstable [[homotopy groups of spheres]] with [[John Coleman Moore|John Moore]] and [[Frederick R. Cohen]].
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Levi |first1=Ran |title=The work of Fred Cohen |journal=Geometry & Topology Monographs |date=7 April 2009 |volume=13 |pages=529–546 |doi=10.2140/gtm.2008.13.529 |arxiv=0904.1315|s2cid=16382169 }}</ref>

Neisendorfer's book ''Algebraic Methods in Unstable Homotopy Theory'' was described by Stephen Theriault in the ''[[Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society]]'' as "very well written and organized". Theriault recommended it as a text for students preparing to conduct research in unstable homotopy theory and as a reference for experts.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Theriault
 | first = Stephen
 | title = Algebraic methods in unstable homotopy theory (New Mathematical Monographs 12) By Joseph Neisendorfer
 | journal = Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society
 | volume = 43
 | issue = 5
 | pages = 1028–1031
 | date = October 2011
 | doi = 10.1112/blms/bdr066
}}</ref>
